title: India's Refiners Are Redrawing the Oil Map. The Iran War Forced Their Hand.
excerpt: Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL are eyeing crude from Guyana, Brazil and the US to reduce their dependence on the Middle East — a shift that could be the most significant in India's energy history.
body:
For decades, India's crude oil supply chain ran on a simple logic: buy from the Middle East, negotiate annual term contracts, and keep the tankers running. The Iran war broke that logic in weeks.

Now, as the dust settles on a four-month conflict that shut down the Strait of Hormuz and sent India's energy establishment into crisis mode, the country's biggest refiners are making moves that could fundamentally reshape where India gets its oil — and how much it pays for it.

## The Shock That Changed Everything

At the peak of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in late February, India's oil supply chain was stretched to breaking point. The Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes — was effectively closed.

Behind the scenes, Indian officials scrambled. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar flew to the UAE. Prime Minister Narendra Modi followed weeks later. National Security Adviser Ajit Doval travelled to Saudi Arabia. Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri went to Qatar. The objective in every meeting was the same: keep fuel supplies moving.

India managed. LPG tankers were given safe passage through Iranian-controlled waters after direct appeals. Russian crude, permitted under US sanctions waivers, helped fill gaps. But the experience left a mark.

## The New Playbook



> **"India imports nearly 85% of its crude requirements, and the Middle East has traditionally accounted for the lion's share."**


According to an Outlook Business report, India's three largest public-sector refiners — Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum — are now actively looking at crude from producers they have historically bought little from: Guyana, Brazil and the United States.

The logic is straightforward. India imports nearly 85% of its crude requirements, and the Middle East has traditionally accounted for the lion's share. The Iran war exposed the concentration risk. A single geopolitical event in the Gulf can threaten the energy supply of 1.4 billion people.

Guyana and Brazil offer light, sweet crude that Indian refineries can process efficiently. US crude — particularly from the Permian Basin — has become increasingly competitive since America lifted its export ban a decade ago. And none of these routes pass through a conflict zone.

## The Russian Cushion

Russia has become a significant stopgap. US sanctions waivers have allowed Indian refiners to increase Russian crude imports, and the Rosneft-backed Nayara Energy refinery in Gujarat has been running almost entirely on Russian oil. But analysts see this as a temporary arrangement rather than a permanent solution — Russian supply carries its own political risk, and the waivers could be revoked.

Even Indian Oil, the country's largest state refiner, has been setting up a new trading desk in partnership with commodities giant Vitol Group — a move to modernise procurement and gain more flexibility in spot markets.

## Building a Buffer

Separately, an oil ministry panel is now studying plans to build strategic petroleum, LPG and liquefied natural gas reserves large enough to cover roughly a month of domestic consumption. India currently maintains strategic petroleum reserves at three locations — Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur — but their combined capacity covers only about 10 days of consumption. The new plans would triple that buffer.

## The Iranian Window

Meanwhile, a parallel track is opening up. After Washington granted Iran a 60-day sanctions waiver as part of the nascent peace deal, middlemen and traders have been approaching Indian refiners with discounted Iranian crude — $3 to $4 per barrel cheaper than comparable regional grades.

National Iranian Oil Company representatives and intermediaries from Singapore and Dubai have contacted refiners directly. Iranian Petroleum Minister Mohsen Paknejad discussed potential supplies during his visit to New Delhi for the BRICS Energy Ministers' Meeting last week.

But Indian refiners have limited room to absorb new supply in the near term. Most have already locked in contracts through August, and their existing Middle Eastern suppliers are pressing them to honour annual commitments. Payment mechanisms for Iranian oil also remain unclear — the last two cargoes India received in April were settled in Chinese yuan.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

India's crude oil import bill is the single biggest variable in the country's fiscal math. It affects the rupee, inflation, petrol prices, government spending capacity, and ultimately the growth rate that determines everything from job creation to the stock market. When India's refiners start diversifying away from the Gulf — a move described as potentially the most significant change in decades — it signals a structural shift in how the country manages its most important economic vulnerability. For NRIs watching India's economic trajectory, the oil map matters as much as the GDP number.

*Sources: Reuters, Outlook Business, OilPrice.com, The Indian Eye*
